title: Put down the matches: why higher education needs evolution, not revolution
summary:
This blog outlines the speech that Rose Stephenson, Director of Policy and Strategy at HEPI, delivered to the recent Universities UK conference. Rose had been asked to debate John Blake of the Post 18 Project on the future of higher education. John was asked to argue for revolutionary change to the sector, while Rose was […]

The post Put down the matches: why higher education needs evolution, not revolution appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog outlines the speech that Rose Stephenson, Director of Policy and Strategy at HEPI, delivered to the recent Universities UK conference. Rose had been asked to debate John Blake of the Post 18 Project on the future of higher education. John was asked to argue for revolutionary change to the sector, while Rose was asked to make the case for a more evolutionary approach. You can read John’s remarks here: https://post18.co.uk/is-another-future-possible/.

This session works best if I’m honest. Higher education has significant structural problems, and government has offered little serious response. So my provocation will focus on being honest about what’s working and being very careful about the case for burning it down.

Imagine another UK sector where most customers ended up wealthier and healthier as a result of their interactions with it. Where it was the second best in the world at attracting foreign investment for one of its products, bringing billions of pounds into the UK each year. Where it was also ranked second in the world for supplying that product to serving heads of state. Where it was globally recognised and punched above its weight for creating knowledge. And where, as a bonus, it made its customers more democratically engaged. We would not call that sector a failure. We would not want to start again. That would be madness.

That sector is higher education. We must protect it.

Measuring student choice

I’ve been asked to speak on student choice specifically. A lot has been said about how flawed that choice really is; that a seventeen-year-old can’t make an informed decision and that too many are studying so-called ‘Mickey Mouse’ degrees. So, that got me thinking: how do we actually know if student choice is working?

We could ask this question financially. The recent IFS report on graduate earnings shows that most students do make choices that pay off. And for those who don’t, I welcome the push to put more of that data on UCAS, so applicants are making an informed choice.

We could ask if students would make that choice again. Ninety-three per cent of students would attend higher education again, but with only two-thirds picking the same course and institution. So again, there is something about supporting informed choice here.

Nicola Dandridge’s hindsight research on graduates finds that ninety-seven per cent would go again, though only around half would repeat the same choices – and that figure blends genuine regret with people whose careers simply took them somewhere they didn’t expect. There is real work still to do unpicking which is which.

I think this points not to government intervention, but to better advice. Students are already turning to AI to help choose their course. Perhaps we could explore building a sector-backed AI model that responds to personalised applicant information and is trained on verified data rather than the open internet.

Where choice puts real pressure on the system

We could also ask about the impact of student choice on the overall market. A growing share of domestic students are applying to high-tariff institutions every year. While the Government talks about collaboration, the system we’ve built rewards fierce competition. Your job as leaders and mine as a governor is to fight for our institution’s survival, not my neighbour’s. The upcoming reduction in the 18-year-old population, combined with the changing approach to recruitment, is squeezing medium- and low-tariff institutions hard.

It is likely that some of these institutions will close. That will be devastating for students, staff, alumni and communities. However, the impact will not be even. Lose an institution in London, and applicants still have dozens of others within reach. I live in rural Gloucestershire, where most people can reach at best one institution by public transport. The same is true across Cumbria, Cornwall and other rural regions. At a time when fewer students can afford to move away from home, losing that one institution would shut the door to in-person HE provision for whole communities, and the downstream impact would absolutely gut the regional economy.

However, I don’t think the fix is to predetermine student choice. Telling an applicant they cannot go to the University of HighTariffShire, and must go instead to the University of MiddleTariffShire might not even work and certainly isn’t the only lever we have. Institutions doing genuine regional heavy lifting

Institutions doing genuine regional heavy lifting – for skills, for employment, for the local economy – should be supported to keep doing it, even at a smaller scale, that is financially challenged. Yes, that raises a flag on institutional autonomy. But where an institution is embedded in delivering the workforce a strategic authority needs for its own growth plan, there’s a real case for that support. Devolution gives us a genuinely new lever here that’s worth exploring properly.

Are the right incentives in place?

I was also asked whether the right incentives exist to meet the needs of the economy. ‘Incentive’ might be generous. What’s actually pushed institutions this hard towards economic outcomes is four things:

a regulatory system (in England) fixated on graduate outcomes;

a student population, rightly, focused on return on investment (imagine being twenty, with no family financial backing, navigating today’s rental market, and tell me students shouldn’t care about their RIO);

a UK economy that has barely grown in years, which is honestly why we’re all having this discussion and the resulting challenges in the graduate jobs market;

and, in places, a maturing devolution settlement providing mechanisms to evolve course and curriculum design to respond to real local need. Government is already pulling levers here too, restricting maintenance loans and LLE funding to courses in predicted growth sectors.

Evolution, not revolution

So my proposal is for evolution, not revolution:

keep the focus on outcomes,

engage seriously with strategic authorities; particularly for institutions that serve their local areas,

make sure student choice is genuinely informed, and

back new models of delivery for underserved areas and lifelong learners.

There is no white knight coming. International student numbers are not bouncing back. Tuition fees are not rising in real terms. This is probably the most sympathetic government towards higher education we are likely to see for some time. Given the demographic changes ahead, the sector will very likely get smaller – and it has never done that before. We have only ever grown, and we have been good at it. There is no blueprint for shrinking well.

So, some institutions will get smaller. Most will get leaner. This will likely include mergers and the closure of some.

Regional institutions should be protected, but that protection has to be earned through the role they play.

The difference between shrinking well and shrinking badly isn’t luck; it’s leadership: the pace at which we choose to evolve, our willingness to hand policymakers solutions instead of waiting for them, and our courage to accept the trade-offs the whole sector needs, not just the ones that advantage our own institution. This is challenging, but it is essential to protect the many things we do so well.

title: Stanford Scientist Wins Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
summary:
Stanford Scientist Wins Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
Susan H. Greenberg Tue, 10/06/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Susan H. Greenberg
full_text:
Karl Deisseroth, a professor of bioengineering and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University, was among the trio of researchers awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday.

Deisseroth, along with Peter Hegemann from Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg, also in Germany, won “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics,” according to the Nobel Foundation. Essentially, that means they figured out how to turn on and off the individual nerve cells in a brain using light—known as optogenetics—which can lead to greater understanding of how memories, feelings and behaviors are formed.

“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.

Each scientist focused on a different part of the process.

“I couldn’t be happier because the trio that the committee picked spans the progression from the early algal explorations all the way to advanced neuroscience experiments, so this prize really captures the full journey of discovery,” Deisseroth told Stanford.

Deisseroth missed the initial call from the Nobel committee, which came at 12:27 a.m. Pacific time. The committee members then called his wife, Michelle Monje, a pediatric neuro-oncologist at Stanford. “May we speak with Karl?” they asked.

The three winners will divide the roughly $1.2 million prize equally.

title: 4 Lessons on Lower-Income Student Success
summary:
4 Lessons on Lower-Income Student Success
Joshua.Bay Tue, 10/06/2026 - 03:00 AM

College access is only part of the challenge for lower-income students. Here’s what recent research says about supporting them through graduation.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Getting lower-income students to graduation requires more than making college affordable at the point of enrollment.

Recent research highlights how food insecurity, unexpected expenses and other financial pressures can threaten persistence, even as it offers lessons from institutions with strong outcomes for Pell Grant recipients about how to support students through graduation.

Here are four takeaways for colleges looking to address the barriers that can stand in the way of student success, especially for low-income enrollees.

Look beyond college access.

Higher education has long been considered an avenue to economic mobility, but lower-income students continue to face disparities in college access and degree completion. Those gaps have persisted even as college enrollment has expanded, raising questions about which institutions are most successful at supporting lower-income students through graduation and into the workforce.

Recent research from the University of Wisconsin at Madison, published in AERA Open, identifies colleges and universities where Pell Grant recipients enroll and graduate at relatively high rates, face small completion gaps compared to their higher-income peers, and see strong earnings after college.

Drawing primarily on federal data from 1,462 four-year institutions from 2015–16 through 2019–20, researchers evaluated colleges across three dimensions: access for Pell recipients, degree completion and postgraduation earnings. They also examined whether institutions graduated Pell recipients at higher rates than expected based on their student populations, resources and other characteristics.

The researchers identified 149 high-performing-Pell institutions that met their criteria. At those colleges, Pell recipients had an average graduation rate of 76.5 percent, compared with a 50 percent median across the broader sample. The average graduation gap between Pell and non-Pell students was 3.8 percentage points, compared with 13 points across the sample.

Taylor Odle, assistant professor at UW Madison and co-author of the study, said the institutions identified as high-performing represent a wide range of colleges and universities, challenging assumptions about where strong outcomes for lower-income students are possible.

“Good work is being done across the higher education sector,” Odle said. “What we want to do is show that there is data out there that complicates some of the stories that we’ve always had in our minds, but that data can be used to make very high-stakes decisions in support of these lower-income students.”

Recognize the academic toll of financial strain.

For some college students, covering basic needs means taking on debt. Some put expenses such as food, housing and transportation on credit cards, and many carry unpaid balances as they manage the costs of college. Recent research from Trellis Strategies suggests that financial strain can follow students into the classroom, making it more difficult to focus on their studies.

The data comes from the postsecondary research and consulting firm’s 2025 Student Financial Wellness Survey, which drew more than 65,000 responses from undergraduates at 153 institutions in 23 states, including over 32,000 credit card users. It found that 54 percent of respondents reported using a credit card in 2025, up from 43 percent in 2018.

Fewer than half of student cardholders (47 percent) pay their balance in full each month, the survey showed. Among those carrying a balance, 88 percent said they worried about covering basic monthly expenses, compared with 61 percent of those who pay in full. Some 60 percent of students carrying unpaid balances also reported difficulty concentrating on schoolwork due to financial stress, compared with 43 percent of those who pay their balances in full.

Bryan Ashton, managing director at Trellis Strategies and co-author of the report, said the findings highlight the financial pressures students can face as the cost of living rises while their options for borrowing to cover expenses outside of tuition remain sparse.

“We have limitations on what we can do with student loans, especially federal student loans, because of caps,” Ashton said. “But when indirect costs go up—cost of living, housing, food, transportation—we don’t really see the ability for students to increase borrowing without going to the private market. So sometimes credit cards become the one way that students can close that indirect-cost gap.”

Close the emergency aid gap.

An unexpected expense is one of the most common reasons students stop out of college. Research has shown that emergency aid—a timely grant that helps a student cover an unexpected cost—can greatly improve the odds that they stay enrolled and complete a degree or credential.

However, an analysis from the Hope Center for Student Basic Needs at Temple University found that despite growth in emergency aid programs on college campuses, far fewer students are receiving that assistance.

Using data from Trellis’s Student Financial Wellness Survey, the analysis found that the share of students receiving emergency aid fell from 44 percent in fall 2021 (when colleges were distributing federal COVID relief funds) to 4 percent in fall 2025—a decline of roughly 90 percent.

Muhammad Kara, policy and research analyst at the center, said emergency aid is designed to help students respond quickly to an unforeseen financial crisis. Unlike traditional financial aid, which is packaged months before a term and disbursed on a fixed schedule, emergency aid can be distributed when a student faces an immediate expense.

Kara said the decline in students receiving emergency aid suggests colleges are either failing to publicize available support or operating programs that are too limited in scope or funding to meet student need.

“These have real-world applications,” Kara said. “If a student can’t pay a medical bill or afford food or housing, they’re really not going to be focused on their academics.”

Address food insecurity before it derails students.

Pell Grant recipients are nearly twice as likely to experience food insecurity as students who do not receive the federal grant, according to an analysis from the Institute for Higher Education Policy.

Drawing on data from the Beginning Postsecondary Students Longitudinal Study, the analysis found that 42 percent of Pell recipients experience food insecurity, compared to 22 percent of students who do not receive Pell Grants.

Marián Vargas, former IHEP assistant director of research and co-author of the report, said food insecurity can make it harder for students to stay enrolled and complete their degrees.

“Students should not have to choose between eating and staying enrolled in college,” Vargas said. “Supports like Pell and SNAP are essential tools for expanding opportunity and supporting student success, but right now the supports are not keeping pace with students’ financial realities.”

“Sustained investment in affordability and basic needs support can help more students persist and complete their degrees, and it’s absolutely essential if we want to create a new socioeconomic reality in this country,” she added.

title: As the mother of a student in Paris, I see what’s happening: reasonable demands met with awful violence | Helen Massy-Beresford
summary:
The debate around the schools protests is angry and polarised. I fear this is a foretaste of how election tensions next year will play out

  • Helen Massy-Beresford is a British journalist who lives in Paris

It would be tough to argue that the demands of France’s protesting high school students are not reasonable ones, worth taking to the streets for: investment in crumbling schools, replacing absent teachers, reducing class sizes and overstuffed timetables, and bridging the inequality gap between schools in different areas.

The protests across the country on Tuesday, which demonstrators dubbed l’acte III (Act 3), or la grande mobilisation, were billed as the most dramatic day of action yet, with more school blockades and a march through central Paris in the afternoon. More than 400 schools closed preventively, including my elder daughter’s, a combined collège (for 11- to 15-year-olds) and lycée.

Helen Massy-Beresford is a British journalist and editor who lives in Paris

Continue reading...
full_text:
It would be tough to argue that the demands of France’s protesting high school students are not reasonable ones, worth taking to the streets for: investment in crumbling schools, replacing absent teachers, reducing class sizes and overstuffed timetables, and bridging the inequality gap between schools in different areas.

The protests across the country on Tuesday, which demonstrators dubbed l’acte III (Act 3), or la grande mobilisation, were billed as the most dramatic day of action yet, with more school blockades and a march through central Paris in the afternoon. More than 400 schools closed preventively, including my elder daughter’s, a combined collège (for 11- to 15-year-olds) and lycée.

At 11 she’s too young to be involved, and after her reports of fireworks, burning bins and smoke as she and her friends ran in through the gates one day last week, I must say I’m relieved – no matter how worthwhile the cause. It was business as usual on Friday (a few more parents picking up their children than would normally, though), while on Tuesday morning, with school closed, the gates were blocked with bins and about 50 lycéens (one dressed as Batman) were there, wielding their banners. The atmosphere was calm, with attention shifting to the big protest march through the city due later in the day.

While there have been some cases of violence from protesters, heavy-handed police methods have been severely criticised. In one incident, in Tours, a 16-year-old boy lost sight in his right eye, an injury the city’s prosecutor said was consistent with a rubber bullet. In a particularly dark turn on Monday, and in circumstances that are not yet entirely clear, a lycée student lost his hand at a demonstration in Lens, northern France. A police investigation is under way.

As the protests have grown in scope, the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has promised the government will listen and try to meet the main demands – but that’s unlikely to mean suddenly freeing up billions to invest in schools that have gone underfunded for years, as the videos posted online of rat-infested, flooded or crumbling classrooms testify.

The political debate surrounding the escalating social movement is angry and polarised: a foretaste of the how the country’s April 2027 presidential election is likely to play out. The high school movement comes at an already tense time, with France’s government once again trying to push through a budget full of spending cuts without a parliamentary majority.

Last year, to get the budget over the line, the government had to use special constitutional powers to bypass the need for a parliamentary vote. This year’s budget, due for a vote in November, includes pension and healthcare cuts aimed at helping to plug the seemingly bottomless budget deficit – and is likely to be just as problematic for the government.

The intensity of the protests has prompted a mudslinging match between two of the favourites for the first round of the presidential elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, is vocally on the side of the protesters (many of whom will vote for his party when old enough) but rejects the narrative that his party stirred up the unrest. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is using the protests to call for an anti-riot law. She’s clearly not following the advice of the Socialist party leader, Olivier Faure, who during a presidential primary debate among leftwing candidates urged people not to fall into the classic rightwing trap of focusing on the violence while ignoring the cause of the protests.

Faure made reference to the proverb of the wise man pointing at the moon and the fool looking at his finger: “look at the moon, not the finger,” he said – and it’s a sensible message for all the wannabe presidents. Many of the lycéens protesting today will be voting for the first time next April.

Even if Le Pen is now looking at the finger, she certainly shouldn’t be written off for next year’s election; her message seems to be resonating with a large number of French citizens and she is the clear favourite for the first round of the presidential elections. We’ve been here before: if the polls are correct, it will be Le Pen’s third second-round run-off. The difference is that in 2022 and 2017 she was up against Emmanuel Macron – a centrist candidate who voters from across the spectrum could get behind to block her, even if many reported holding their nose at the ballot box.

As things stand, that may be harder for many in 2027. Le Pen’s opposition is fragmented, with several potential candidates still in the running on the left and centre right – and because of that, Le Pen’s second-round adversary may prove easier for her to beat, to the benefit of absolutely no one.

Everything stayed quiet yesterday in my north-east Paris neighbourhood. But in the centre of the city, organisers say some 100,000 people turned out (the interior ministry estimated 56,000). Under a blazing early October sun, huge – and mainly calm – crowds gathered in Place de la République and marched to Place de la Nation to chant and wave placards. As the main crowd dispersed, some small groups clashed with police as the sun was setting.

For now, the movement’s momentum seems to be building, not receding. Some politicians are realising that, six months away from a fraught election, they should listen to their future voters.

title: Brazil election: Authoritarian right gain an edge, fueled by voter apathy and discontent
summary: Far-right lead in the presdential race and landslide victories in legislative and local elections have affective, value-based, and political-ideological explanations.
full_text:
The far-right bubble that has seen populist rightist figures elected across Latin America spilled over and flooded the ballot box in Brazil’s general elections held on Oct. 4, 2026 – fueled by a discontented and distrustful public. In spite of voting being mandatory in the country for literate citizens aged 18 to 70, a wave of disengagement swept across 33.4 million voters who did not cast a ballot — 21% of the electorate.

It was the highest abstention rate since 1998. We still need to investigate what produces bubbles and waves in contemporary politics, but I have a few tentative hypotheses about this process.

This kind of ebb and flow has three dimensions: affective, value-based, and political-ideological. The affective dimension is one of depressive sentiments. Three feelings predominate: resentment, anger and political fatigue. Anger stems from the fear of losing what one has and from the aversion generated by feeling neglected by the political leadership in power. Under affective polarization, it turns into hatred.

Political fatigue, or social exhaustion, is a state of social weariness and disenchantment arising from the perception that political institutions are no longer capable of providing effective governance or fulfilling long-term commitments. Those who hold governmental power are the primary targets of this adverse sentiment among voters.

Resentment has been captured by the digital far-right. It uses falsehoods and the filtering enabled by algorithms to manipulate these resentments.

Across the world, fear of the social dislocations brought about by the digital revolution, still in its infancy, fuels depression. The far-right exploits this by stoking hatred against the “other side”, portraying it as responsible for the processes causing loss of social status or threatening further loss.

Reaction to social inclusion

The values and worldviews dimension reflects a strong reaction among people across all social strata to the behavioral changes in society and social inclusion of historically marginalized groups. Inclusion rekindles what I have called the “casa-grande mentality” (a reference to the master’s house in the slavery system that existed in Brazil until the end of the 19th century) in my new book, A Terceira Margem do Ipiranga: Povo, Democracia e Futuro_ (“The Third Margin of Ipiranga River: People, Democracy and Future_”, not published in English).

As for the behavioral changes in society that began in the 20th century and accelerated in the 21st, it has provoked a conservative wave in values and in personal, social, sexual and political behavior, reinforced by extremist religious movements, particularly evangelical neo-charismatic movements. This is clearly a reactive, or reactionary, turn aimed at restoring “traditional values”.

Political fatigue is directly related to the transformations already reshaping society as the digital revolution advances. New interests, demands and needs are emerging that governments and institutions are unable to represent or address.

A social majority is gradually taking shape, driven by widely differing motivations but sharing the same weary sense that the “establishment,” or political elite, has nothing to offer but more of the same.

This sense of political fatigue prompts a search for something “different,” something that presents itself as new. The far-right is mistaken for a force of innovative change, even though I would argue that it fails to understand the present and carries a backward-looking vision, focused on an idealized past rather than the future.

We have seen this shift to the popular right in recent years across countries around the world, from Europe to Asia and Latin America, including more recently Argentina, Chile and Colombia in the region. How this sociological model should be adjusted to explain what is happening in each country is a question that, in my view, still requires further research. Clearly, every country experiences this moment in its own way.

In Brazil, political fatigue is directly associated with the country’s multiparty system. The Workers’ Party (PT) of current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva remained in power for 14 uninterrupted years (2003-2016) and, following former president Jair Bolsonaro administration (2018-2022), returned to office for at least another four years (2023-2026), once again under Lula.

During this period, the alternative that had provided a functional rotation in government, represented by the Brazilian Social Democracy Party (PSDB) – which along its history shifted from social democracy toward social liberalism – lost its ability to field competitive presidential candidates. This happened first in the electoral rupture of 2018 – the election that brought Jair Bolsonaro to power – and again in 2022, with Lula’s return.

Meanwhile, PSDB and another center-right party, the Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB), dwindled in size and influence, while the right-wing Democrats (DEM) merged with the Social Liberal Party (PSL) — the party Bolsonaro was affiliated when elected in 2018 and subsequently abandoned by him — to form União Brasil, or Brazil Union.

The disappearance of functional alternatives to Lula’s PT opened the way for the far-right. The Liberal Party (PL) occupied this space in Congress and became competitive in presidential elections. But PL is not committed to the democratic system, and on its rise it swallowed up the right wing parties that, unlike it, were committed to democracy.

Democracy at risk

My general hypothesis is that nowadays no government, regardless of its political persuasion and in any democratic society, is capable of satisfying a discontented and distrustful public. Within the democratic field, the most likely outcome is high turnover, with a growing number of incumbents failing to win reelection. The far-right can remain in power only if, once in government, it dismantles democratic institutions, especially those responsible for providing the checks and balances necessary to preserve the integrity of democracy.

Brazil is entering a territory of high risk and democratic threat because the far-right emerged from the elections with formidable strength in Congress, particularly in the Senate, while also securing the largest bloc in the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house in Brazil’s Congress.

Brazilian far-right now has the means to attack the legal framework underpinning democratic institutions. The crisis within the Federal Supreme Court (STF), deeply divided internally and with several justices owing public explanations for inappropriate conduct of its members, further aggravates the situation.

Moreover, four Supreme Court justices are due to retire upon reaching the mandatory retirement age, and one seat is still vacant since the Senate rejected President Lula’s nominee earlier this year. With that, the Court risks being overtaken by the far-right on the short term, which would further neutralize its role as a guardian of the Constitution and its checks and balances.

title: Moving Beyond the ‘Presentation Parade’: Designing Onboarding That Actually Teaches
summary:
​​​What words would you use to describe your back-to-school educator gathering? Kick off? Launch? Retreat? Presentation Parade? All too often, we educators forget to model what we know about how learning works when we gather for back-to-school work.   In my work helping to onboard ~125 Undergraduate Learning Assistants (ULAs) each August, our gathering has evolved […]

The post Moving Beyond the ‘Presentation Parade’: Designing Onboarding That Actually Teaches appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
​​​What words would you use to describe your back-to-school educator gathering? Kick off? Launch? Retreat? Presentation Parade?

All too often, we educators forget to model what we know about how learning works when we gather for back-to-school work.

In my work helping to onboard ~125 Undergraduate Learning Assistants (ULAs) each August, our gathering has evolved over the last few years from a 3-hour “presentation parade” to interactive sessions modeling (and reflecting on) practices we want the ULAs to exemplify in their work and equipping them with the institutional information, skills, and context to be successful beginning their work.

Here’s how we made the change:

Backwards Design

What do you really want folks to take away from your gathering? What are your reasons to gather and how would you know if they had been met? We apply these backwards design principles in our teaching, and they are equally applicable – though often absent – for our meetings with educators.

If your gathering is primarily to disseminate information, it’s unlikely you need to gather. Consider instead sending a well-written and formatted email or a short video with the information you need to share.

If you want folks to use or do something with the information you want to share, shift the focus of the session to an activity that helps them build both the knowledge and the skill to do that something.

From Policies to Practice

The ULAs I work with need to be aware of several campus offices (Care Team, Ombuds, etc.) as well as University policies that apply to them as employees involved in education (FERPA, RVSM, etc.). Historically, we invited folks from each office or unit responsible to uphold the policy to come briefly explain their piece. Most presenters paused for questions, but it was primarily one-way communication, from the presenter to the room full of ULAs trapped in this presentation parade.

What I really need is for the ULAs to recognize that they are in a situation where one of those policies or campus office is relevant, and to know how to respond accordingly and/or ask for help. In collaboration with folks in the MSU Department of Mathematics, we developed a case study based, small group activity. Each group was assigned to find information about one campus unit or policy (links were provided) and discuss how to respond to a case study situation relevant to that office. We had one group for each unit or policy share out what they learned and how they would handle the case study scenario. These scenarios often elicited insightful, nuanced questions from other students and thus opportunities for deeper conversations about their work – the responsibilities, challenges, and opportunities. A brief but summative handout was provided at the end of the activity so that folks had a take-home resource that they could refer to later.

By more clearly articulating the goals of the session and better aligning the session activities, I shifted us from a passive parade to focused, small group work. This change gave the young educators the opportunity to build new knowledge, share their learnings with others who need that information, and awareness of realistic scenarios in which their new knowledge will be relevant.

Model the Work

Most educators have sat through a painfully ironic lecture about active learning.

Instead of propagating that experience, consider what approaches you might want to model for your educators – new and with various levels and types of prior experiences.

To help facilitate the small group activity described above, we hired and trained “ULAs to the ULAs” to support effective small group work in a large learning environment. These senior ULAs modeled the practices that we hope the ULAs enact in their work: moving between groups to start conversations, checking for understanding, encouraging participation from multiple folks, supporting the lead instructors’ sense of the progress and vibe of the room, and answering questions.

Most of the ULAs have been students in a course supported by a ULA, but that doesn’t mean that they were paying attention to what the ULA was doing during those class meetings. By modeling these teacher moves during the onboarding and taking a moment for folks to reflect on the work that the ULA trainers were doing, we helped model and surface in real time the kinds of inclusive, active strategies we hire the ULAs to incorporate across the 17+ courses that they support.

Honor Your Educators

Do you expect your educators to be human-centered, flexible, inclusive educators? If so, then you need to exemplify that in your back-to-school gathering.

What information about scope, timing, logistics, flexibility, and expectations would most help your educators physically, mentally, and relationally be present?

Provide the full agenda – including those new, clear goals – with timing cues ahead of the gathering. A week ahead would be best but aim for 2-3 business days minimum.

Provide information about where you are meeting: how to enter the building, where the room is in the building, where the bathrooms are near your meeting room, if there are outlets and power strips available in the meeting room, etc.

Intentionally plan (and staff) for flexible modalities, either async or hybrid.

If applicable, provide information about what sorts of beverages and food will be available, how allergies and food sensitivities will be accommodated.

Plan shorter sessions (1 hr max) with breaks between sessions.

While not exhaustive, the above list exemplifies some ways that leaders can show care for their educator community via planning and proactive clarity.

Conclusion

When we stopped thinking of onboarding as a place to deliver information and started treating it as a place to model learning, everything changed.

Our ULAs left not just with handouts, but with habits.

And that’s the invitation for all of us: to design our gatherings so that they look like the learning we hope to see.

For Reflection

How could you more carefully align the activities of your gathering with your actual reasons to gather? What part of your typical back-to-school gathering might be performative and thus not actually necessary?

What sorts of actions and strategies do you hope your educator community enacts in their classrooms? How could you model that in your back-to-school gathering?

What sorts of information and planning would exemplify the kind of care and inclusive, community-centered practices that are essential to your community?

Dr. Rachel Barnard is a teaching-focused faculty at Michigan State University, where she works with Undergraduate Learning Assistants (ULAs) across undergraduate STEM courses. Her work centers on educator development, inclusive teaching practices, and designing learning environments that help students and educators thrive. She is particularly interested in how institutions can better support early-career educators through intentional onboarding, reflective practice, and community-centered program design.

title: France's conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests
summary: Prime Minister Lecornu is pledging to improve schools at a time when the government seeks to save billions. France's dilemma can be seen across the EU: How to cut spending when citizens are demanding more from the state?
full_text:
France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is unlikely to have had a quiet weekend. For almost two weeks, students across France have been protesting, angered by class cancellations, overcrowded classrooms and run-down school buildings. The protests have increasingly been overshadowed by serious clashes with police.

At the same time, the government accuses the left-wing party La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting the protests for political purposes and fueling the blockades.

On Friday, Education Minister Edouard Geffray tried to ease tensions by meeting with student representatives. It was unsuccessful.

Instead, a nationwide day of protest took place on Tuesday.

On Sunday evening, the prime minister took charge of the crisis. In a letter to several ministers, Lecornu called for concrete proposals: Class cancellations should be addressed more quickly, school buildings should be upgraded to cope with hotter summers, and the controversial university admissions system "Parcoursup" should become more transparent.

Initial decisions, along with funding and a timetable, are expected to be announced this month. But Macron's ally Lecornu faces one key problem: He has to promise young people more government support while his government is imposing an austerity budget on the entire country.

A signal to the markets

Last Thursday, the government submitted its 2027 budget proposal to parliament. The budget deficit is expected to fall from a projected 5.4 % of economic output this year to 5% in 2027. To make up the shortfall, the government plans to make spending cuts worth billions of euros. France is already subject to an EU excessive deficit procedure and is expected to bring its budget gap back toward the 3% limit set by the European Union.

"It is an austerity budget," says Eileen Keller of the Franco-German Institute (dfi) in Ludwigsburg. At the same time, the draft is a signal to the financial markets. The government wants to show "that it is taking responsibility" and lay out a path toward reducing the deficit.

No majority in sight for the budget

The government plans to cut spending by the state itself, local and regional authorities, as well as in the social sector. Overall, Paris aims to reduce the budget by around €54 billion ($60.8 billion) compared with previously projected spending plans. Pensions alone are expected to make savings to the tune of around €5.5 billion, and more cuts are also planned in healthcare.

Whether the budget will actually be passed in its current form is still wide open. Lecornu's government does not have a parliamentary majority and relies on opposition votes. But with presidential elections coming next spring, an austerity budget is even less attractive to the opposition than it would otherwise be.

More money for schools — and more protests

The issue of education in particular shows that France's problem cannot be reduced to the formula "The state is cutting too much." The education budget is set to increase by around €1.2 billion in 2027. At the same time, the government expects around 1.7 million fewer schoolchildren by 2035.

For Keller, this contradiction shows that money is only part of the problem. Public dissatisfaction is linked to what she calls "priorities" and the fundamental direction of the education system, including the transition from school to higher education.

Financing education is getting more costly

The difficult outlook for France is compounded by another factor: the financial markets. For many years, France was used to financing its high levels of debt at relatively low interest rates. But those days are over. The yield on 10-year French government bonds has risen sharply in recent weeks. At times, the spread over German government bonds widened to around 1.5 percentage points, the highest level since the euro debt crisis in the 2010s. The business daily Les Echos ran the headline on Monday that the country was in the "eye of the cyclone."

Market skepticism is hitting France at a particularly difficult time. With debt at around 119% of economic output, France is almost twice as heavily indebted as Germany, whose debt ratio stands at around 64%.

Step by step, old government bonds that were issued at very low interest rates are increasingly having to be replaced with new and more expensive debt. The effects of this are clearly visible in the 2027 budget. Estimated around €74 billion, the government will have to spend more on its interest payments than it can afford to spend on schools or defense. According to Finance Minister Roland Lescure, interest payments already consume more than half of the overall budget deficit.

Keller stresses that it is therefore crucial that France continues to be seen by investors as a "credible debtor." These days, however, that credibility depends on more than just economic data.

Markets keeping a close eye on election campaigns

In spring 2027, the French will elect a new president. "The election campaign, which is now gaining intensity, is being watched by the financial markets," Keller says. In an analysis for the dfi, she puts the need for fiscal consolidation at between €75 billion and €160 billion, depending on the calculation.

From the markets' perspective, political consensus on the need for the nation to tighten its belt would be helpful. But, at present, there is no sign of clarity. How the burden will be shared in the future is instead likely to become a central issue in the election campaign.

A French problem with a European dimension

France is an especially acute case. But many other European countries are also currently grappling with fiscal consolidation and how to finance the state. Europe wants to spend more on defense, modernizing its infrastructure and transitioning to renewable energy sources. At the same time, citizens still expect a certain standard of education, pensions and healthcare.

In France, this conflict can be observed almost in real time. The issue is not only whether the government can respond to the demands of young people, but also whether it can avoid further violence. In Paris, many are wary of the prospect of a new broad-based social movement, like the Yellow Vests protests of the past. For Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, the coming days will be a major test.

This article was originally published in German.

title: Ideenwettbewerb Digitale Souveränität: Preisträger stehen fest
summary:
Digitale Souveränität wird an den Hochschulen im DACH-Raum aktiv gestaltet: Dieses Bild zeichnen die zahlreichen guten Einreichungen für unseren einschlägigen Wettbewerb. Die Projekte „openEduSuite“ (Marburg), „KIT-GenAI-Kit“ (Karlsruhe) und „LLMduckt“ (Graz) konnten die Jury am meisten überzeugen.

The post Ideenwettbewerb Digitale Souveränität: Preisträger stehen fest appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
In unserem Ideenwettbewerb Digitale Souveränität hatten wir Ende Juli zum Mitmachen eingeladen. Insgesamt 19 Projekte reichten eine Bewerbung ein – von der Projektskizze bis zum bereits laufenden Großvorhaben. Die thematische Bandbreite reichte dabei von Künstlicher Intelligenz über Governance-Fragen bis hin zum souveränen Datenmanagement.

Die Jury zeigte sich beeindruckt von der hohen Qualität der Einreichungen. Außerdem auffällig: Wie erwartet beschäftigten sich viele Einreichungen mit KI, aber auch abseits davon gab es preiswürdige Einreichungen. Die Siegerprojekte werden jetzt mit Partnern aus dem HFD-Netzwerk zusammengebracht, um die guten Ideen skalieren zu können und auch in anderen Hochschulen nutzbar zu machen. Wir danken allen Einreichenden für die rege Beteiligung – wir bleiben mit allen gerne weiter in Kontakt und finden Wege, das Thema der Digitalen Souveränität gemeinsam weiterzutreiben.

openEduSuite (Tobias Weiß / Philipps-Universität Marburg)

Die openEduSuite ist ein modulares, Kubernetes-natives Ökosystem, das Bildungsdienste als austauschbare Komponenten bereitstellt. Jeder Dienst kann einfach ersetzt oder ergänzt werden – ohne die gesamte Plattform zu ändern.

Die Jury sagt: „Genau das, was als Grundlage gebraucht wird. Endlich eine Infrastruktur für deutsche Hochschulen!“

Innovationsraum für generative KI am KIT – GenAI@KIT (Andreas Sexauer / Karlsruher Institut für Technologie)

Das Projekt verfolgt das Ziel, den kompetenten Einsatz generativer KI am KIT zu fördern und gleichzeitig Risiken verantwortungsvoll zu adressieren. Es soll ein Entwicklungsrahmen für die Nutzung von generativer KI am KIT entwickelt werden, der sowohl die technologische Infrastruktur als auch praxisorientierte Anwendungen voranbringen soll. Durch die Kombination von explorativen Ansätzen und konkreten Use Cases soll die nachhaltige Nutzung von KI sichergestellt und die Weiterentwicklung der Technologie aktiv mitgestaltet werden. Ein besonderes Augenmerk liegt darauf, auch Kolleg:innen ohne Vorkenntnisse den Zugang zu generativer KI zu erleichtern.

Die Jury sagt: „Alle relevanten Aspekte für den Fokus auf KI sind adressiert. Verständlich, umfangreich, sensationell!“

LLMduckt (Benedikt Brünner / Technische Universität Graz)

Lehre mit KI-Sprachmodellen braucht nicht nur Chatoberflächen, sondern auch Zugänge zur Programmierschnittstelle – und dafür für jede Studierende und jeden Studierenden einen eigenen Schlüssel. LLMduckt stellt beides bereit: Lehrende wählen die Modelle, das TeachCenter verteilt die API-Schlüssel an den Kurs.

Die Jury sagt: „Ein schönes Projekt und gut übertragbar auf einzelne Hochschulen. Die Perspektive der Veröffentlichung als Open Source Software ist ein Bonus.“

Karin Vosseberg ist Professorin für Informatik und Wirtschaftsinformatik an der Hochschule Bremerhaven. Seit 2021 ist sie Aufsichtsratsmitglied der HIS eG.

Matthias Bandtel ist Geschäftsführer des Hochschulnetzwerks Digitalisierung der Lehre Baden-Württemberg (HND-BW). Etwaige regionale Befangenheit wurde deswegen im Vorfeld der Jurytätigkeit angesprochen; Seine Stimme ist deswegen bei der Diskussion zum Preisträger aus dem Karlsruher Institut für Technologie nicht eingeflossen.

Reinhard Karger ist Sprecher des Deutschen Forschungszentrums für Künstliche Intelligenz.

Simone Rehm ist CIO und hauptamtliche Prorektorin für Informationstechnologie an der Universität Stuttgart.

Uwe Reckzeh-Stein ist bei der Hochschulrektorenkonferenz (HRK) Projektreferent für das Hochschulforum Digitalisierung. Dort betreut er die Community, organisiert deren regionale Vernetzung und koordiniert die AG-Arbeit seitens der HRK. Nach einer Ausbildung zum Technischen Assistenten für Informatik, studierte er Katholische und Ökumenische Theologie in Münster und Bonn. Er arbeitete als Vikar in Karlsruhe und als wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter an der Katholisch-Theologischen Fakultät der Uni Bonn. Zwischen 2017 und 2020 forschte er zu Kirchen- und Militärgeschichte.

title: Continuarea și extinderea implementării în România a programelor FLEX Global și FLEX Abroad Global în anul școlar 2027 - 2028
summary:
Continuarea și extinderea implementării în România a programelor FLEX Global și FLEX Abroad Global în anul școlar 2027 - 2028
Tue, 6 Oct 2026 - 12:00
daniel.tomoni Tue, 6 Oct 2026 - 11:57
Etichete
comunicate de presă
FLEX
Categorie
Comunicate de presă
full_text:
Marți, 6 octombrie 2026, ministrul Educației și Cercetării, Mihai Dimian, și președinta & directoarea executivă a American Councils for International Education, Lisa Choate, au semnat Memorandumul de Înțelegere privind acordarea de burse în anul școlar 2027 - 2028, în cadrul programelor FLEX Global (Future Leaders Exchange Global) și FLEX Abroad Global.

Semnarea Memorandumului are loc în baza mandatului de negociere și semnare aprobat de Guvernul României la 1 octombrie 2026 și asigură continuarea programelor de schimb educațional în Statele Unite ale Americii și respectiv, în România, în anul școlar 2027 - 2028.

Prin noul acord, până la 70 de elevi români vor putea beneficia de burse pentru a studia, timp de un an școlar, în licee din Statele Unite ale Americii, iar până la 20 de elevi americani vor putea studia în România. Numărul burselor acordate elevilor români crește astfel semnificativ față de anul școlar 2026 - 2027.

Bursele vor fi finanțate în mod egal de Guvernul României, prin Ministerul Educației și Cercetării, și de Guvernul Statelor Unite ale Americii, prin Biroul pentru Afaceri Educaționale și Culturale al Departamentului de Stat al SUA.

Procesul de selecție pentru anul școlar 2027 - 2028 este prevăzut să înceapă în luna noiembrie 2026.

Mihai Dimian, ministrul Educației și Cercetării:

„Educația creează legături durabile între oameni și, prin oameni, între țări. Aceasta este una dintre valorile cheie ale programelor FLEX Global și FLEX Abroad Global. Prin memorandumul semnat astăzi, continuăm un program care și-a dovedit valoarea pentru tinerii români și, în același timp, îl extindem semnificativ: până la 70 de elevi români vor avea oportunitatea de a studia timp de un an în Statele Unite ale Americii. Investim astfel în educația și în potențialul lor, precum și în parteneriatul dintre România și Statele Unite ale Americii. Le mulțumesc partenerilor noștri americani și American Councils for International Education pentru contribuția lor esențială la continuarea și dezvoltarea acestor programe.

Dragi tineri, vă încurajez să candidați! Iar dacă veți fi selectați, reprezentați cu mândrie comunitatea din care veniți și, la întoarcere, folosiți ceea ce ați învățat pentru a contribui la dezvoltarea ei.”

Lisa Choate, președinta și directoarea executivă a American Councils for International Education:

„România investește propriile resurse în acest program, FLEX Global, iar acum îl extinde. Acest lucru spune multe despre modul în care Bucureștiul privește viitorul relației sale cu Statele Unite, pentru că investițiile comune creează parteneriate durabile. Elevii americani și români care participă la program vor deveni antreprenorii, profesioniștii și liderii din sectorul public care vor transforma acest parteneriat în rezultate concrete. Americanii care cunosc România vor ajuta companiile și instituțiile din SUA să aibă succes aici. Absolvenții români ai programului care înțeleg Statele Unite vor sprijini companiile românești să investească și să se dezvolte în Statele Unite. Totul începe cu educația. Îi mulțumesc ministrului Mihai Dimian pentru angajamentul său față de acești tineri și față de viitorul pe care îl vor construi.”

FLEX Global este unul dintre cele mai importante programe de schimb educațional pentru elevi derulate între România și Statele Unite. Implementat în România începând cu anul 2015, programul le oferă elevilor de liceu selectați pe criterii de merit posibilitatea de a petrece un an școlar în Statele Unite, unde studiază într-un liceu american și locuiesc alături de o familie-gazdă.

Interesul elevilor români pentru acest program a crescut constant. În perioada 2015 - 2025 au fost depuse peste 18.000 de candidaturi, iar finaliștii au provenit din aproape toate județele țării și din comunități de dimensiuni diferite. Numai în ultima rundă de selecție numărul candidaturilor a fost de aproximativ 3.000, reprezentând un nivel record pentru România.

FLEX Abroad Global, implementat în România din 2024, le oferă elevilor americani posibilitatea de a petrece un an școlar în România, de a studia într-un liceu românesc și de a locui alături de o familie-gazdă. Programul contribuie astfel la dezvoltarea schimburilor educaționale și a legăturilor directe dintre tinerii și comunitățile din cele două țări. Cele două programe sunt administrate de American Councils for International Education, organizație nonprofit cu experiență internațională în implementarea programelor de schimb educațional.
